Power Supply Disrupted in British Virgin Islands Amid Electric Utilities Workers’ Strike

ROAD TOWN, British Virgin Islands, June 14 — Widespread power outages affected thousands of residents and businesses across the British Virgin Islands on Friday as a strike by electric utilities workers entered its second day, causing significant disruption to the territory’s energy supply.

The walkout, organized by the BVI Electrical Workers’ Union, began early Thursday morning after negotiations with management at Virgin Islands Power & Light broke down over wage increases and safety concerns. Union representatives said more than 85 percent of the company’s workforce had joined the industrial action.

As a result, major generating plants on Tortola and Virgin Gorda have been operating at reduced capacity, leading to rolling blackouts and intermittent service in several communities. According to the Ministry of Natural Resources and Labour, at least 14,000 customers experienced partial or total loss of electricity since Thursday.

“Our members are committed to providing reliable service, but we cannot continue under these conditions,” said union president Carlton Malone at a press conference in Road Town. “We urge management to return to the table with a fair proposal.”

Virgin Islands Power & Light said in a statement it “regrets the inconvenience caused to customers” and is “implementing contingency plans to maintain essential services.” The company did not provide a timeline for full restoration of power, but a spokesperson said limited technical staff are working to stabilize the grid.

Local authorities have urged residents to conserve energy and report outages as the strike continues. “We are monitoring the situation closely and remain in contact with both parties,” said Permanent Secretary of Labour Denise Harrigan. “The government encourages a swift resolution to minimize further hardship for the public.”

The strike comes as the islands enter the summer tourism season, a period of typically high electricity demand. Analysts warn that prolonged disruptions could strain backup generation systems and complicate efforts to maintain critical infrastructure.

A joint statement from the Chamber of Commerce and Hotel Association highlighted the growing concerns among businesses. “Reliable electricity is essential for daily operations and public safety,” the statement said. “We call on all stakeholders to resolve this matter urgently.”

As of Friday afternoon, union leaders said they had not received a new offer from management. Negotiations are expected to resume over the weekend.
